explain.say: In 138 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, west to find allies against the Xiongnu, the horse-riding power of the steppe. He was captured and held for about ten years, escaped, and came home thirteen years later with news of unknown kingdoms. Look at the network: the world his journey opened.

explain.say: Here is a wall on the northern frontier in 3D. The Han extended frontier walls to guard the Silk Road, though most of the brick wall standing today was built later, under the Ming. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

explain.say: Start at the right, Chang'an, today's Xi'an, the Han capital. Silk went west through Dunhuang, the desert gateway, to Sogdian traders near Samarkand, then on through Parthia in Iran. Horses came back east; Emperor Wu prized the fast horses of Ferghana. Can you spot the link carrying Buddhism from India?

explain.say: Now the map. Silk passed from hand to hand across more than 6,000 kilometres, and wealthy Romans wore it, though Rome and Han China never met directly. Why might traders in the middle prefer the two ends never to meet?

How big was Han China? See the sizes. A census in 2 CE counted about 57.7 million people, one of the oldest surviving censuses in the world. Rome at about the same time had perhaps 45 million, an estimate. By 140 CE the Han count was about 49 million. Why might a census number fall without many deaths?

draw.text: Roman figure is a modern estimate; Han figures are censuses.

explain.say: The German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen named the Silk Road in 1877. See the debate: Valerie Hansen argues most trade was local and small, but ideas, religions and technologies like paper travelled far. Superb. Challenge: name one idea that travelled these routes and is still with us.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Small trade, huge exchange of ideas.

faq.a: A network of overland routes linking China, Central Asia, India, Iran and the Mediterranean, active from the Han dynasty. Silk, horses, spices, glass and silver moved along it, and so did religions, technologies and diseases.
The capital of the Western Han dynasty, near today's Xi'an, and later of the Tang. It was the eastern starting point of the overland routes west.

An envoy sent by Emperor Wu of Han in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu. Captured for about ten years, he reached Central Asia and returned around 125 BCE with knowledge that opened Han contacts westward.
asks: Why did Emperor Wu send Zhang Qian west?

faq.q: How many people lived in Han China?
faq.a: The census of 2 CE recorded about 57.7 million people, a figure based on household registers. Later counts, such as about 49 million in 140 CE, also reflect how well the state registered people.
asks: What did the Han census show?

faq.q: Was the Silk Road a single road?
faq.a: No. It was a shifting web of routes and relay trade, and the name was coined only in 1877. Historians like Valerie Hansen argue that most trade was local and small-scale, while ideas and technologies travelled very far.
asks: Did merchants travel the whole Silk Road?

facts: The Han dynasty ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE.
A Han census of 2 CE recorded about 57.7 million people.
Ferdinand von Richthofen coined the term Silk Road (Seidenstrasse) in 1877.

quiz.say: Why did Emperor Wu send Zhang Qian west?
quiz.why: Emperor Wu wanted the Yuezhi as allies against the Xiongnu steppe confederation.

wrong.1: Trade grew afterwards, but the mission was diplomatic and military.
wrong.2: Buddhism reached China later, from the first century CE.

quiz.say: The 2 CE Han census counted 57.7 million people and the 140 CE census about 49 million. Roughly how big was the drop?
quiz.show: From 57.7 to about 49 million is a drop of about…
quiz.why: 57.7 minus 49 is 8.7, so about 9 million, partly due to war and partly to weaker registration.

wrong.1: That would bring the count down to under 38 million.
wrong.2: The gap is much larger than 1 million.
